balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Phillips 66: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Phillips 66: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Phillips 66: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Phillips 66: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

segmentProfit.title: Segment profit (before-tax)
segmentProfit.content:
Phillips 66 reports pre-tax income for five segments: Refining (crack-spread economics), Midstream (fee-based pipelines, terminals and NGL fractionation/export), Chemicals (50%-owned CPChem JV, equity-method), Marketing & Specialties (fuel/lubricants resale) and Renewable Fuels (Rodeo/Humber, credit-sensitive).

For Phillips 66: Refining is the smallest share of revenue (~25%) but the largest and most volatile share of profit -- a 2026 margin spike drove it to roughly three-quarters of segment pre-tax income through Q3. Marketing & Specialties is the opposite: the biggest revenue line (~62%) on consistently thin, stable margins. Renewable Fuels swung from a FY2025 loss to a large Q3 2026 profit purely on LCFS/RIN/SAF credit values.

What to watch:

  • Refining's share of total segment profit versus its share of revenue -- it is the swing factor in any given quarter
  • Midstream's steady, less cyclical contribution as the buildout (Western Gateway Pipeline, Coastal Bend) continues
  • Renewable Fuels profit tracking regulatory credit prices rather than fuel volumes

refiningThroughput.title: Crude throughput and refining margin
refiningThroughput.content:
Crude throughput (thousand barrels per day, mbd) is how much crude the refineries actually processed; refining margin ($/bbl) is the realized crack spread captured on that throughput, net of all refining costs.

For Phillips 66: throughput is capacity-constrained and moves slowly (LA refinery closure, turnarounds); margin is the commodity-driven variable that swung from ~$11/bbl in FY2025 to ~$38/bbl in Q3 2026 on industry-wide capacity rationalization and Mideast supply disruption. Margin, not volume, explains most of the earnings swing.

What to watch:

  • Margin reverting toward mid-cycle levels once the current capacity-tight environment eases
  • Capacity utilization (in the KPI cards) confirming throughput isn't being held back by unplanned downtime

marketingMargin.title: Marketing fuel margin: US vs international
marketingMargin.content:
The cents-per-gallon margin Marketing & Specialties earns reselling fuel at wholesale/retail, split between the US network and the international network (Europe, including the Germany/Austria business partially divested in Dec 2025).

For Phillips 66: this is the thin, high-volume margin that makes M&S ~62% of revenue but a small share of profit -- it can go negative in a quarter (seen in both US and international legs in the data) even while Refining posts a record margin, since the segments are economically distinct.

What to watch:

  • Negative margin quarters that aren't offset by a strong Refining quarter
  • International margin volatility against a shrinking international footprint post-divestiture

midstreamVolumes.title: Midstream volumes: NGL fractionated and pipeline
midstreamVolumes.content:
NGL fractionated and pipeline volumes (both mbd) are the physical throughput behind the fee-based Midstream segment -- gas processing, NGL fractionation/export and pipeline transport that behave like toll roads rather than commodity-margin businesses.

For Phillips 66: Midstream is ~12% of revenue but a steadier profit contributor than Refining; the Permian/Gulf Coast buildout (Coastal Bend fractionation, the Western Gateway Pipeline JV) is meant to keep these volumes growing even if refining margins normalize.

What to watch:

  • Volume growth tracking the announced capacity additions, not just commodity prices
  • Midstream segment profit (see the segment-profit chart) rising in step with volumes

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Phillips 66: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Phillips 66: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Phillips 66: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Phillips 66: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Phillips 66: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
